title: She remembers, and he comes
hook: Satyavati tells Bhishma about her firstborn and calls Vyasa with a thought: why Hindus repeat God's name
carry: smarana: remembering god is itself devotion

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati asked Bhishma to break his vow, and he refused. Satya, a word given is sacred.

Bhishma has refused her, but he doesn't leave her empty-handed. He tells old stories of lines carried on in hard times, when a learned man was invited to father children for a house that had none. Find such a man, he says. And Satyavati, the text says, smiles, and her voice falters with shyness. Then the queen mother tells her stepson something she has carried since before she ever saw a palace.
screen: `FIND A LEARNED MAN.` → `SHE SMILES, AND FALTERS.` → `A SECRET FROM THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: She tells him about the boat: the sage Parashara, the mist on the Yamuna, the son born on an island. That son, she says, is Dvaipayana, the great sage people call Vyasa, and when he left he promised to come whenever she thought of him. If you agree, I'll think of him now. Bhishma agrees. Satyavati thinks of her son, and that's all it takes. Vyasa appears at once, the text says. He bows to his mother; she weeps and holds him, and tells him plainly what the house needs. Look back over the week: a vow and a boon, a baby in a fish, a boat and a fragrance, a proud son fallen, Amba's choice, Bhishma's no. And the one door left open is the one she opened herself, years ago, on a river. Now the teaching. In Hindu devotion, remembering isn't small. It has a name: smarana. When the boy Prahlada lists the ways to love God in the Bhagavata Purana, remembering comes third, right after hearing and singing. That's why so many Hindus keep a name of God going through the day: Ram, Ram while cooking, beads in the morning, Krishna's name before sleep. It's called naam smaran, remembering the name, or japa when it's counted on a mala. Many teachers say the idea isn't that God is far away and must be summoned. Remembering turns you toward the one who was near all along. Satyavati thinks, and her son comes. A devotee remembers, and the holy is there.
screen: `THE BOAT, TOLD AT LAST.` · `SHE THINKS OF HIM. HE COMES.` · `A WEEK, LOOKED BACK ON.` · `SMARANA: REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `NAAM SMARAN.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus repeat a name of God, often on a mala of a hundred and eight beads. Choose a name that's dear to you: Ram, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, or Om. Say it softly, once with each slow breath, for a couple of minutes. If you don't pray, choose a word you love, like shanti, peace, and do the same. When your mind wanders, that's fine; remembering again is the practice.
Satyavati. The fisherman's daughter who became queen mother of the Kurus, and called her son home by remembering him.
Your line: smarana, remembering God is itself devotion. Next, the birth of the cousins. Day seven hundred twenty-one, done.

howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a mala of 108 beads for japa, repeating a name of God or a mantra once on each bead; others simply keep a name like 'Ram' going under their breath through the day.

chat.meaning: Vyasa promised to come whenever his mother thought of him, and he did. In bhakti, remembering God's name, smarana, is itself a way of being near.
